cues.text: In 1803, two American negotiators were in France
hoping to buy a city.
They wanted New Orleans, a port near the mouth of the Mississippi River.
Farmers could float their goods down that river and ship them out to sea.
If another country could shut the port, it could cut
them off from their markets.
Napoleon's government offered the Americans something much bigger:
all of Louisiana.
The purchase roughly doubled the size of the United States on paper.
It also opened a fight over what would happen as the country grew.
Would slavery spread into those lands?
Every new state could change who held power in Congress.
And the people already living on the land had never been asked whether
it was France's to sell.
The United States had begun as thirteen British colonies
along the Atlantic.
After years of disputes over taxes and who had the right to impose them,
the colonies went to war with Britain and declared
independence in 1776.
They claimed that people had equal rights, even as slavery remained
legal and millions of people had no political voice.
In the peace treaty of 1783, Britain recognized the new
country, with the Mississippi as its western boundary.
Indigenous nations lived on both sides of that line.
For the American government, the immediate problem
was that the river's outlet at New Orleans lay outside its borders.
Napoleon had wanted Louisiana as part of a revived French
empire in the Americas.
But a revolution in France's Caribbean colony of Saint-Domingue, now
Haiti, was wrecking his bid to restore control there.
With the colonial plan falling apart and war with Britain
looming, he agreed to sell.
France transferred its claims to Louisiana.
The people who lived there still had their own governments, communities
and lands. As settlers moved west, new states could apply
to join the Union.
Each state, large or small, would send two members
to the Senate, one of the two chambers of Congress.
As long as the number of states that allowed slavery matched
the number that banned it, neither group had a majority there on its own.
Then Missouri applied to join as a state where slavery would be legal.
Congress agreed to bring in Maine as a free state
and Missouri as a slave state.
It also drew a line through the rest of the Louisiana Purchase,
banning slavery north of that line, with Missouri as the exception.
The compromise kept the balance for a time.
Meanwhile, the government was opening land to settlers in places
already inside the nation's claimed borders.
The Cherokee fought removal through petitions and the courts.
In 1838, soldiers forced thousands from their homes
and sent them west.
Many died during or as a result of the removal remembered
as the Trail of Tears.
The map of the country barely changed.
The people who could remain on that land did.
Then the external borders began to move again.
Texas broke away from Mexico in 1836 and joined the United States
nine years later as a slave state.
Mexico disputed the annexation, and the two governments disagreed
over where Texas ended.
American troops entered the disputed land between the two claimed borders.
After they clashed with Mexican forces, Congress declared war.
To the northwest, the United States and Britain settled their competing
claims in Oregon by treaty.
The war with Mexico ended differently.
After American troops took Mexico City, Mexico ceded a vast
area that included California and much of what is now
the American Southwest.
The United States stretched from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
These diplomatic lines ran through lands where Indigenous nations
still lived. The new territory made the old fight urgent again.
Congress admitted California as a free state in 1850 and passed a tougher
federal law requiring the return of people who had escaped slavery.
Four years later it organized the territories of Kansas and Nebraska
under a new rule.
Settlers would determine whether slavery was allowed there,
even though the old Missouri line had barred it.
People on both sides rushed into Kansas.
Rival groups fought over elections, and then they fought with guns.
The line on the map could no longer hold the peace.
The fight reached the Supreme Court.
Dred and Harriet Scott, an enslaved couple who had lived
in places where slavery was prohibited, had sued for their freedom.
Dred's case went to the Supreme Court.
He lost. The Court's majority also said Congress had no power
to ban slavery in federal territories.
The compromise that had once kept slavery out of part of the West
was now under attack from both lawmakers and judges.
In 1860, Abraham Lincoln won the presidency on a platform that opposed
the spread of slavery.
Leaders in the slaveholding South feared that as more free states joined,
they would lose the power to protect slavery.
South Carolina declared that it was leaving the Union.
Other slave states followed and formed the Confederacy.
Federal troops still held Fort Sumter in South Carolina.
In April 1861, Confederate guns opened fire on the fort.
A country that had spent decades pushing its borders
outward was now fighting over whether it would remain one country at all.
The Union went to war to keep the country together.
Enslaved people forced the war to confront a second question.
At Fort Monroe in Virginia, three men escaped slavery and asked the Union
garrison for refuge.
When a Confederate officer demanded them back, the Union commander refused.
More people came.
They were taking action for their own freedom, and the army had to decide
what it would do when they arrived.
In 1863 Lincoln declared enslaved people
free in areas still in rebellion.
Where the Confederacy held the ground, enforcing that declaration depended
on what happened in the war.
The Mississippi mattered again.
The Confederacy still held Vicksburg, a fortified city on the river.
Union troops surrounded it, and people inside sheltered
from shells in caves dug into the hills.
Vicksburg surrendered. Days later the Union captured the last Confederate
stronghold on the river, separating Confederate territory west
of the Mississippi from its main forces in the east.
The river that had helped drive the Louisiana Purchase now cut
through the rebellion.
The war continued for almost two more years.
In April 1865, Confederate general Robert E. Lee
surrendered his army to Ulysses S. Grant at Appomattox.
Other Confederate armies surrendered later.
By the end of the year, the Thirteenth Amendment had abolished slavery
throughout the country, with an exception for punishment
after a criminal conviction.
The Union had survived.
The map kept changing.
The United States bought Alaska from Russia and later annexed Hawaii
after the overthrow of its monarchy.
Alaska and Hawaii became states in 1959,
bringing the number to fifty.
Other places under American sovereignty, including Puerto Rico,
remained territories. Back in 1803, the negotiators
had gone to France for a way to get goods out to sea.
They came home with a deal that changed the country's scale.
As the United States pushed west, it took land from Indigenous peoples,
and every new state reopened the question of where slavery would be allowed
and who would have the power to protect it.
The war kept the country together and led to the abolition of slavery.
The people who had fought for freedom still had to fight
to exercise their rights inside those borders.
